#933. A clash to savour at Ffos Las on Wednesday

Having been declared to clash at Cheltenham over the weekend, Old Park Star and Sober Glory both swerved commitments at Prestbury Park in favour of more suitable conditions in South Wales on Wednesday, and we are treated to a fascinating contest with Baron Noir also thrown into the mix.

Cheltenham's loss is Ffos Las' gain on Wednesday as old rivals Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir are set to face-off on chase debut and At The Races' Declan Rix previewed the contest.

You always need a bit of luck in this game, no matter what your role or ability. While the elements have unfortunately conspired against those at Exeter so far this season, Ffos Las is the beneficiary of what they are calling The Welsh Arkle on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports Racing.

The race got a huge boost with the somewhat surprise addition of 2026 Supreme Novices' Hurdle winner Old Park Star, a high-profile non-runner on Cheltenham's Saturday card due to the ground being deemed too quick. His inclusion means we have a huge early season clash with an old foe in Sober Glory, last season's unlucky Supreme runner-up.

The inclusion of Old Park Star is no doubt bad luck for those connected to Sober Glory et al; after all, the Henderson-trained horse was meant to run last Saturday, but it's a huge stroke of luck for Ffos Las and indeed, Sky Sports Racing. Exciting early season clashes like this are incredibly rare for novice chasers in Britain - and in general given the monster that the Cheltenham Festival has morphed into - so it's understandable there is a bit of a buzz around the industry ahead of the five-runner Golwg Gwendraeth Beginners' Chase, due off at 13:18pm.

As of 8.37am on Tuesday, on the back of 16mm since 6pm on Monday, the ground is officially Good (good to soft in places), but with significant rain due. According to the BHA site, tomorrow's forecast reads as, 'blustery with persistent rain, heavy at times throughout the day'. Hopefully it leads to beautiful soft ground which the horses will get through nicely.

As the official ratings and betting suggests, Old Park Star (155; 4/6) and Sober Glory (153; 15/8) are the standouts and are set to renew their rivalry having served up a fantastic Cheltenham Festival curtain raiser in March, along with Mydaddypaddy back in third. At the line, the winning margins were 1½ lengths and a nose, with the also reopposing Baron Noir (146; 10/1), Wednesday's third favourite, a further 6 lengths back in fourth.

Wednesday's prices and a glance at the formbook in black and white could lead you down the garden path of just siding the unbeaten hurdler Old Park Star, but replaying the final flight of their Supreme clash is wise, given it had such a significant impact on the race.

Heading to the last in the Supreme, Sober Glory looked to have everything in trouble with a good 1½+ lengths lead before he put in an extra stride, hit the hurdle and landed steeply, losing critical momentum. It was a huge shame for his connections because up to that point he had jumped so well and looked the best horse in the race going to the last.

That mistake cost him dearly, along with many punters having been a huge gamble from 16/1 in the morning to an SP of 9/2. The Philip Hobbs & Johnson White yard clearly felt like they had their charge in great order, produced him beautifully on the day only for that famous last flight on the Old Course at Prestbury Park to scupper a dream start to the 2026 Festival.

His disappointing run 31 days later at Aintree is easily excused on the back of a long season after a huge Cheltenham run and now with his attentions turned to chasing, this former Irish point-to-point winner for Cormac Doyle rates an exciting prospect for the upcoming campaign for owners Brocade Racing.

Standing in his way again is fellow six-year-old Old Park Star, who, to be fair, didn't exactly ping the final flight in the Supreme himself, also putting in an extra stride which led to the son of Well Chosen landing awkwardly but crucially, not losing as much momentum as Sober Glory.

That saw him stay unbeaten in four hurdle starts, after wins at Kempton, Cheltenham and Haydock, showing good versatility in terms of the tracks he could handle along with also displaying tactical adaptability. Having jumped right in places on debut, his hurdling got better and slicker as the campaign progressed and he looked a straight-forward character throughout.

Having been put away after Cheltenham, Old Park Star's attentions now to turn chasing, a game he possesses the physical scope and athleticism for, although unlike Sober Glory he has no point-to-point background. While not ideal, it's possibly a good sign that Nicky Henderson was willing to pitch him into Grade 2 company at Cheltenham on chasing debut before the ground ruled him out.

A horse said to be big and weak last season, there could be much more to come from Old Park Star, his trainer's comments of 'he's still a shell of a horse' last year continually playing on my mind. If he was able to achieve what he did last season when weak, you cannot but be excited about him after another summer on his back.

Never miss a story with all the latest racing news, interviews and features on your phone. Find out more

Baron Noir is certainly no no-hoper against Old Park Star and Sober Glory, with 7½ lengths and 6 lengths, respectively, to find with the leading pair, especially if he has settled down for a summer's break and/or fences curb his keen-going ways.

It's in his breeding to be highly-strung, being by Vadamos out of a Dylan Thomas mare, but he's a horse with plenty of ability and it was a clear sign of the belief his trainer Alan King had in him to run in a Supreme when only rated 130.

While essentially well-held at the line, the six-year-old shaped better than the distance beaten, not getting up the hill as well as his Wednesday rivals. With that in mind, the much flatter nature of Ffos Las should suit.

He too has no point-to-point background, but with the King yard ticking along nicely, he is certainly worth a market check.

See the latest horse racing news, interviews and features from Sky Sports Racing

It's not often you would get prices of 33/1 about a Grade 2-winning novice hurdler from the Skelton yard who looks all-over a chaser on novice chase debut, but that's the task facing Carlenrig. His odds are not just about the horses he is taking on, but also the trip, mind.

A winner of the Grade 2 Bristol Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham last December, he showed a good attitude to win over that 3m trip. On the back of that given his unexposed nature, he looked a big player in the River Don Novices' Hurdle at Doncaster 42 days later - despite carrying a penalty - but having been a stinking drifter (4/1 out to 14/1), fell two out when his race looked to be run.

The former winning Irish pointer picked up a small injury that day and hasn't been seen in 298 days so this looks like a starting point to get his campaign up and running.

Stablemate Bobby's Nelson has his first run for the Skeltons and should be more at home over this 2m trip. He also looks a chaser physically and his three-quarter of a length defeat to Baron Noir last December at Uttoxeter doesn't half look bad now; indeed, you could argue he is overpriced at 80/1 on that effort, but is probably best watched.

In truth, this looks a race to watch for the future, but if forced to have a bet, at the prices, it would certainly be SOBER GLORY. I don't think it's far fetched to say he looked the best horse in the Supreme before his final flight mistake, and with his point-to-point background, might have a jumping experience edge over Old Park Star. That said, the Hobbs and White yard are only operating at a 5% strike-rate currently, for all they've had plenty of others run well. Either way, I am very much looking forward to seeing how all these horses take to fences.

#932. SNL Alum Heidi Gardner’s Boyfriend Ray Tintori Dead at 43

Saturday Night Live alum Heidi Gardner’s boyfriend Ray Tintori died at age 43. The filmmaker was known for directing MGMT's "Time to Pretend," "Kids" and "Electric Feel" music videos.

Heidi Gardner is navigating an unimaginable tragedy.

The Saturday Night Live alum's boyfriend Ray Tintori has died, according to TMZ. He was 43.

A spokesperson for the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner confirmed to E! News their department is investigating Tintori's death, adding in a Nov. 16 statement that a "cause and manner of death are pending further study.”

E! has reached out to Gardner's reps for comment but hasn't heard back.

Tintori was a director known for his work with MGMT, helming music videos for the rock band's 2008 smash hits "Time to Pretend," "Kids" and "Electric Feel" as well as 2024's "Dancing in Babylon." He also directed The Killers' 2009 "Spaceman" music video and the visuals for Arcade Fire's 2017 single "Chemistry."

The son of film editor John Tintori and late script supervisor Mary Cybulski, the filmmaker was a founding member of Court 13, a New Orleans-based, non-profit arts collective that produced the Oscar-nominated 2012 movie Beasts of the Southern Wild.

While Tintori largely kept his personal life out of the spotlight, he did pen a lengthy birthday tribute to Gardner in 2025, describing the Shrinking actress "prettier and more graceful than the moon and by far the coolest person I’ve ever met."

"My favorite song in the world is you singing softly in my ear," he captioned photos of the couple together on Instagram. "My favorite color is the gold at the center of your eyes. I remember the first time we saw each other and how you laughed with your whole body the second our eyes met, and I immediately fell so fast."

"You are the sexiest woman who ever lived, in every single manner of clothing, hair, and old age makeup," he continued. "I’m crushing on you so deep, endlessly. You hold my heart perfectly and love me so proper."

Calling himself Gardener's "boy forever," Tintori added, "You carry the party in your eyes and move like a modern dancer everywhere you go. You are the most genius at making art and surfing the wave with the purest flow I’ve ever seen. The world is a love letter to you."

Prior to her relationship with Tintori, Gardner, 43, was married to Marvel Comics writer Zeb Wells for 13 years before their 2023 split.

"Sadly I went through the end of a relationship, which it feels weird to say end because I also know that person will always be in my life and it will transform in a different way," she shared in a 2024 episode of the The Liz Moody Podcast. "Sending them all the love and respect in the world that I still have for them, but it was just a couple-year period of transition and grief and hope and loss and all of those things."

However, the comedian noted that the breakup also allowed her to get to know herself better.

"During that time, I feel like I never wasted a day in getting to know myself," she added, "becoming a better version of myself and becoming a better friend and future partner."

Gardner was joined by the director as she made her way into an event in the West Village neighborhood of New York in 2024.

The Saturday Night Live alum was joined by Tintori as she attended the Paris Olympics in 2024.

#931. 'Why not have a go?' - the halfway line goal phenomenon

Diego Gomez's shot against Crystal Palace soars over Walter Benitez

David Beckham's goal from the halfway line against Wimbledon in 1996 is one of football's iconic moments.

It helped to catapult the Manchester United midfielder to global stardom and remains a staple of highlight reels.

The impudence to shoot from such a distance highlighted the exceptional talent and character of the future England captain.

Premier League players are now trying their luck from long range more regularly, testing their instinct, precision and technique.

Diego Gomez's stunning 51-metre (56-yard) strike for Brighton against Crystal Palace last month added to the spectacular list in the Premier League, while players in the EFL and FA Cup have contributed their own.

There have already been 19 attempts from over 50 metres this season, on course to beat last season's Premier League total of 26.

Of the 2,733 shots in the Premier League this term, 0.7% of them have come from over halfway - up on 0.3% over the course of last season.

This sample size is admittedly small. And in the case of goals scored from distance lower down the football pyramid, this is data that isn't readily available.

But why are we seeing a growing number of shots being taken from such extravagant distance?

Gomez tried to score from deep in his own half during Brighton's 2-0 win at Sunderland on 10 October.

A week later, he beat Walter Benitez with the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney's 57.6m strike for Everton against West Ham in 2017.

The Paraguayan took advice from Lionel Messi, when the pair were at Inter Miami, to always look to play the ball forward to another level.

It is not just Premier League players who are trying their luck from outrageous distances.

Charlie McNeill scored from halfway for Crewe in their recent 2-1 FA Cup win against AFC Wimbledon.

The on-loan Sheffield Wednesday forward, who played once for Manchester United before leaving Old Trafford in 2024, beat goalkeeper Joe Bursik to open the scoring.

Having done it while at Manchester City and Manchester United's academies, the 23-year-old felt his latest attempt was instinctive.

He told BBC Sport: "Goalies nowadays are always quite high up the pitch - playing a sweeper-keeper role - and I always have a thought if I ever got into that situation to have a go.

"You see it more and more. I had the opportunity so I thought: 'Why not have a go?'

"It was one of those goals. I turned and saw him off his line and in that split-second made the decision to shoot.

"I knew I caught it sweetly and I was following it the whole way in so I knew it had a good chance, but as the keeper was going back I thought he was going to get it.

"When I watched it back it dropped quite early, but as it was getting closer and closer I thought it was going to go over because it went quite high but it dropped in."

Crewe Alexandra's Charlie McNeill talking about the rise in halfway line goals

McNeill joins a growing number of players to have scored from the halfway line or inside their own half over the past 18 months.

Preston Fearon, now on loan at Forest Green, scored two goals from around the halfway line for West Ham Under-21s in their win against Burnley last month.

Gbemi Arubi was barely a stride over the halfway line when he scored for Burton against Peterborough in October.

Last season, Abdul Fatawu (Leicester), Ryan Ledson (Huddersfield), Reyes Cleary (Barnsley), Regan Hendry (Mansfield) and Sammy Braybrooke (Newport) all scored from the halfway line or inside their own half in the EFL.

Two years ago, Chelsea's Moises Caicedo scored from the centre circle against Bournemouth.

Is it all about the goalkeeper's position, as they stand higher up the pitch to either stop opposition attacks or get their own team moving?

"You've got to execute it properly, but it plays a big part. Most keepers are like that, high out the net, because we are playing over the top so they are there first, to get the ball," said McNeill.

"I have always had it in my head and have tried it a couple of times. Although it's not like I do my homework and see he is always off his line. It's one of those instinctive moments."

Paul Robinson scored two goals in his career, one for Tottenham and one for Leeds

Asmir Begovic holds the record for the longest-range Premier League goal when the goalkeeper scored from 95.7m for Stoke against Southampton in 2013.

Two other goalkeepers have scored from their own half: Tim Howard for Everton against Bolton in 2012 and Paul Robinson, who netted for Tottenham against Watford in 2007.

Yet they were flukes rather than by design - similar to Barrow goalkeeper Ben Winterbottom's goal from his own half in their 3-0 National League win at Gateshead on Saturday.

Robinson, who also scored for Leeds against Swindon in 2004, external, feels conceding from distance is now a risk managers are willing to take.

The former England international said: "We've seen the game evolve in the way where the goalkeeper becomes a key figure in starting a pattern of play. The manager wants the goalkeeper at the base of the back three, four or five.

"But then also we're seeing a lot more teams playing with a higher line and the goalkeeper then has to take a higher line of starting position to read the through ball.

"When your team are playing a high line, you obviously have to be further up the field and you're concentrating on where your defensive line is, as opposed to where the football is at times.

"It's one of those things modern-day managers are willing to accept if and when it does happen, because of the way they want their goalkeeper to play.

"We see so many managers come out now and say: 'It's OK. I'm quite happy with them making mistakes. This is the way I want them to play. Blame me because that's what I've asked them to do.'

"We're probably entering that type of territory with it."

With attackers aware of the higher starting position of opposing keepers - a result of teams pressing high - and likely to have been encouraged by the success of other long-range efforts across football, attempts from extreme distance are becoming more frequent in the Premier League this season.

The conversion of efforts from more than 50 metres have increased too - up to 5.3% this season, compared to 1.1% across the previous three seasons combined, with Gomez's strike the first Premier League goal scored from over 50 metres since the 2023-24 season.

It's a small sample size, so more time is required for clearer trends, at least in the Premier League to be established.

But with more long shots being taken and keepers starting higher, there is a suggestion (and hope) we may see more Goal of the Season contenders before the term is out.

#930. Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate

Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career

It was just what they needed at just the right time. For a tricky first half and beyond, Elversberg had been a stone in Borussia Dortmund’s shoe, the promoted side not just keeping the home team at bay but keeping them honest, nourishing ambitions of their own. “The fatigue was clearly visible,” the sporting director, Ole Book, said to Sky after a week which had contained Der Klassiker in Munich and a hard-fought Champions League victory against Betis. “We were a bit too focused on managing the game, which was understandable.”

Enter Felix Nmecha. BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference. It is a gap which has been widened by Dortmund being far from prolific, a facet which looked as if it might undercut their efforts to roll over their visitors on Saturday, especially in the absence of the injured centre-forward Serhou Guirassy.

Somebody was needed to break it open, and it was Nmecha. With two majestic sweeps of his right foot, two rockets from outside the area, he won the game for his team. His decisive moments of elevated quality pulled BVB away from their opponents when the game threatened to drift. “In terms of talent, qualities, and technique, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world,” Book beamed. “Add to that his finishing ability, and there aren’t many who are better.” That they go into the international break neck-and-neck with Bayern is all down to their No 8.

After scoring, Nmecha pointed to the sky, then mimed lifting a crown from his head and placing it on the ground. It was nothing new. He did the same, also in front of the Südtribune, the yawning, world-famous 24,000-capacity terrace in which much of the club’s hardcore support stand, after scoring against Paderborn in September. It was the same celebration that Nmecha used when he struck Germany’s opening goal of the World Cup against Curaçao.

The celebration is a nod to Ballers in God (BIG), the Christian group founded “to use the global platform of football to make Jesus known”, and in particular to their campaign The King’s Return. Yet this latest display provoked a response from BVB’s fan and support department. “When it comes to the values of our club,” it said in a statement the day after the Elversberg game, “discrimination, and the question of what kind of societal image of humanity is given space within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.”

The German public broadcaster ARD has linked BIG to ultra-conservative positions on issues including homosexuality and transgender identity. “Footballers are role models for millions of people, especially children and young people,” the fan and support department continued. “If this reach conveys content that excludes certain groups in society, we cannot dismiss this as merely private religious practice. Where religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, our tolerance for intolerance ends.”

Reports suggest the club has been in dialogue with Nmecha since the Paderborn game, and a statement issued in response to Kicker’s inquiries said those talks would continue – while defending Nmecha. “For Borussia Dortmund, it is essential to take the concerns and needs of the fanbase seriously and to address them,” the club said. “Naturally, we also take the current media coverage and the associated questions and discussions very seriously.” Dortmund appear to have been careful not to use any images of the celebration on the club’s official social channels.

These issues and this dialogue have been almost a constant since Nmecha arrived in June 2023, as a de facto Jude Bellingham replacement. His faith had already been a key part of his social media messaging and, as his transfer from Wolfsburg neared completion, some fan groups voiced their opposition, pointing to Nmecha’s sharing of anti-trans posts by the American rightwinger Matt Walsh, among others. A bright yellow banner was hung outside Signal Iduna Park sprayed with the message “@BVB Steh zu deinen worten”, a message to the club to “stick by your words”. In June 2023 Nmecha posted: “I genuinely love ALL people and don’t discriminate against anyone.”

Dortmund’s motto, or marketing strapline, of Echte Liebe (true love), has been used in the past decade-plus to quantify exactly what makes the club special to audiences all over the world. What BVB believe elevates them is a connection with the fans, a mutual respect and understanding that goes way beyond what has increasingly become a company-customer relationship in modern times. Engaging with supporter concerns is important everywhere in German football and, arguably at Dortmund, there is a commercial imperative to visibly do so.

It was reported widely at the time of his arrival that Nmecha had a clause written into his contract that gave Dortmund the power to fine him if he made social media posts which they felt contradicted the club’s values. The club again had words with the player in 2025 after he posted a message of condolence to the family of Charlie Kirk (Nmecha deleted another post which said Kirk had “peacefully stood up for his beliefs and values”).

Hamburg 3-1 Mönchengladbach, Mainz 1-2 Bayern, Paderborn 2-2 Eintracht Frankfurt, RB Leipzig 5-2 Augsburg, Dortmund 2-1 SV Elversberg, VfB Stuttgart 1-0 Werder, Köln 1-2 Leverkusen, Freiburg 2-0 Union Berlin, Hoffenheim 2-1 Schalke

The difference now is that Nmecha, after a difficult start in Westfalen, has become one of Niko Kovac’s key players, and one of the most recognised in his position in Europe. He scored the first goal of Jürgen Klopp’s Germany tenure, and was linked with big-money moves to the Premier League last summer. So BVB must protect their present, in the sporting sense, their future, in the financial sense, and their very fabric, in terms of their continued relationship with supporters, already strained in recent years by their deal with the arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. For his part Nmecha has responded enigmatically and characteristically, quoting a Bible verse on his socials as a caption to snaps of the game. The one thing the club cannot say is that they never saw this coming.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Bayern remain on top but nothing is easy at the moment, even after their brilliant victory at Atlético in midweek. They closed out a narrow win at Mainz but Manuel Neuer was injured again, sustaining a partial ligament tear of his right foot on the day he became Bayern’s oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days, his sixth substitution in 2026. Whether he will – or should – return is now a fair question, with Jonas Urbig a ready-made replacement. Harry Kane provided assists for both goals to reach double figures in the category, his best assist return in a season already.

The mood was not helped, however, by Uli Hoeness’s latest comments on Jamal Musiala, throwing doubt on whether he can recover his best level on the programme Der Sonntags-Stammtisch. “He’s still getting paid,” the honorary president underlined. “But imagine if FC Bayern were to say what he’s capable of now isn’t what’s stipulated in the contract?”

Even if there was another combination of the El Mala brothers – Malek setting up a goal for Saïd this week – for Köln in the derby with Leverkusen, the game had already been decided then, by a typically classy intervention by Patrik Schick.

#929. The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

A neuron from the human hippocampus. The bushy branches receive signals from other neurons. Credit: Jake Watson and Rebecca Morse-Mora, Jonas group, ISTA

Neuroscientist Lucy Palmer and her team have been waiting days for this moment.

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more

Across the road from her laboratory, at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia, surgeons are removing brain tissue from a person with brain cancer. They set some aside for Palmer to collect and study. It is about the size of a shelled peanut.

A colleague of hers takes the sample, places it in a tub of artificial cerebrospinal fluid and rushes it back to the lab, securing it in a chamber filled with bubbling carbon dioxide and oxygen to keep it alive.

These precious samples can survive for only a day or so before they start to deteriorate, so Palmer’s team wastes no time. Within half an hour of receiving the tissue, they are recording the electrical current passing between neurons as they fire.

Palmer’s group at the Florey Institute in Melbourne is using live brain tissue to understand more about brain cancers and how the activity of neurons influences tumour growth. Her lab, and others using such samples, are doing something rare — measuring how live, working human neurons behave.

Most studies of brain-cell function rely on tissue taken from people who have died or from living animals. Post-mortem human brains, however, preserve only the structure and not the activity of cells, and the brains of other animals might function differently. “As much as we like mice, I don’t want to understand the mouse brain. I want to understand the human brain,” Palmer says.

Slices from a sample of living human brain ready for study.Credit: Emmalyn P. Leonard

Working with living brain tissue from another person is both humbling and a great privilege, she says. “Every sample is precious.” It’s also an artisanal skill: attaching recording equipment to individual neurons requires the neuroscientific equivalent of a gardener’s green fingers. It relies on mastery of a decades-old technique called patch-clamping, which has fallen out of fashion as flashier recording methods have become available.

Despite the barriers, there is increasing interest in this rare resource. The number of studies published about this tissue has increased from just a handful two decades ago to upwards of 40 a year, according to data from Scopus, with the bulk attributed to about ten research teams. Neuroscientists around the world are working with surgeons to access the tissue and keep it alive in their labs for periods of time ranging from 24 hours to a few weeks, investigating the intrinsic electrical properties of cells and how they communicate with each other during both health and disease.

“When looking into a disease, being able to look directly at the human tissue is absolutely vital,” says Palmer.

Neuroscientists have many ways to study the human brain: non-invasive scanning, indirect measures such as blood samples and, after death, in slices under the microscope. They can also study brain function directly in animal models and, very rarely, in people who have electrodes implanted while they are undergoing surgery. But none of those approaches allows scientists to measure and manipulate the activity of individual human brain cells in their natural environment.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

That has changed in the past ten years, says Scott Owen, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. Although people have been studying live human tissue since the 1970s, he says, the field has finally reached a point at which enough is known about the mammalian brain to understand how human brains differ from those of other animals.

His team works with paediatric neurosurgeons to acquire tissue taken from children with epilepsy, cancer or abnormal tangles of blood vessels in their brains. By comparing samples from people with different diseases, the researchers can look for features common to all donors and deduce which are conserved properties of the human brain, rather than artefacts of any one condition.

In a preprint published in September, for instance, Owen and his colleagues found distinct differences in how human pyramidal neurons — big, bushy brain cells that live in the cortex — mature compared with those of mice1. The team analysed neocortex samples from 24 children and teenagers, ranging in age from 9 months to 18 years, and mouse samples from equivalent developmental stages. The study, which is yet to be peer reviewed, looked at patterns in how neurons fire, or spike. It’s known that human neurons are quicker to spike after a stimulus than are rodent neurons and that this might correlate with intelligence. Owen and his colleagues found that human neurons got faster at responding over the course of development, with neurons from teens spiking more quickly than those from children; the opposite happened in mice.

Slices from a sample of living human brain, ready for study.Credit: Rennie Kendrick

When the researchers looked at the genes that might explain how this happens, they found two that increased in expression over time in people, but not in mice. These genes help to create ion channels in cell membranes, which allows signals to travel between neurons. Faults in these genes have been linked to several neurodevelopmental conditions2.

Karri Lämsä, a biophysicist at the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine in Szeged, is also interested in how human neurons fire and how these patterns might change with time and new experiences. His team studies centimetre-wide cubes of the cortex that are discarded during surgeries to enable access to deeper parts of the brain. In a study published last year, they looked at a type of neuron that inhibits others. In these cells, the axon — the main trunk — transmits signals faster and spikes at lower thresholds than in the same cells in mice3. Fast-acting neurons of this type are thought to have a crucial role in complex brain functions.

Lämsä’s team has also been studying how networks of these fast-spiking neurons might change with age. In samples taken from 106 people ranging in age from 11 to 84 years, the researchers found that these circuits become weaker over time and the spikes in electricity travelling across the cell membrane become smaller and slower4. These changes could explain why the human brain becomes less capable of learning and processing information as people age.

Other work using live human tissue has challenged a key assumption about the human brain: that it is a scaled-up version of the mouse brain. Peter Jonas, a neuroscientist at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria in Klosterneuburg, is using live human tissue to understand how brain cells function alone and in networks. Jonas had worked with animal models for more than 30 years when, in 2022, he began collaborating with a neurosurgeon at the Medical University of Vienna. He would receive tiny samples of human brain tissue — mainly from the hippocampus — measuring about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle

Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle

His lab’s work suggests that some properties of the human brain, such as the number of dendritic spines (tiny outgrowths at the end of synapses that connect neurons), follow different scaling rules from those of the mouse. Neurons are also more densely connected in the human neocortex — the area of the brain thought to control higher functions such as decision-making and planning — than in the mouse one, but have fewer connections in the hippocampus. Jonas says that this kind of information can be gleaned only from living tissue.

In a 2025 Cell study examining tissue taken from the hippocampus and cortex, his team also found that the electrical signals transmitted between neurons were more reliable and precise than they were in mouse brains5. The synapses in human brains successfully triggered the receiving cell to fire 90% of the time, compared with a 62% success rate in mice. Computer modelling by Jonas’s team suggests that reliable transmission could set the human brain apart from those of other species. “We are at the beginning of understanding this,” says Jonas.

Meanwhile, Palmer has observed that the excitability of brain cells differs between humans and rodents6, which could be because human dendrites are twice as wide as those of mice. Differences in size also affect how the cells handle information, she says. Larger neurons with longer, bushier branches can form widespread networks, whereas smaller neurons restrict a network to their close neighbours.

Palmer also finds human tissue invaluable for studying disease. Cancers in mouse brains are generally composed of a limited number of cell types, whereas every single cell in a human brain tumour is different. Furthermore, most brain cancer research in mice has focused on one particular type of cancer, called glioblastoma.

Neurons from the human cortex next to their neighbours. Scientists can record from several branches of these complex neurons to monitor their activity.Credit: Jake Watson, Jonas group, ISTA

Using slices of human brain tissue, Palmer and her team have found that cancer cells taken from aggressive tumours were more active than those in slower growing tumours7, boosting signalling and forming more synapses with neurons. The researchers also found that neurons were generally more active in people with aggressive tumours and that this increased activity leads to greater spread of cancer cells, confirming results from animal models.

In a study testing the efficacy of a drug for brain cancer, Palmer’s team also saw changes to excitability and signalling in neurons8. Together, the findings could explain how the drug slows down tumour growth, or halts it entirely.

One of the biggest challenges of working with living human brain tissue is a specialist technique that scientists need to learn. Called patch-clamping, the technique involves pressing the tip of a glass micropipette against the membrane surrounding a neuron and using suction to make a tight seal. A cell’s electrical activity can then be measured through one or several ion channels in the membrane. These measurements are used to study how a neuron behaves in response to different stimuli.

Patch-clamping was invented in the 1970s and is an indispensable tool in electrophysiology. It stands in stark contrast to techniques such as calcium imaging and optical imaging, which allow scientists to measure electrical activity in thousands of neurons at once. These techniques are more expensive but less technically challenging, says Palmer. In comparison, “patch-clamping takes a year to learn and years to understand,” she says. “You never master it.”

#928. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.
