#884. Bryce Dallas Howard Reacts to Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

Bryce Dallas Howard had the best reaction to her Twilight costar Robert Pattinson being named the new James Bond in an exclusive interview with E! News at the 2026 ELLE Women in Hollywood Celebration.

Robert Pattinson, you better hold on tight, spider monkey.

Because after being selected as the new James Bond following a yearslong search, his super stardom is about to reach new heights. But his Twilight costar Bryce Dallas Howard knew he had something special from the start.

“He's a sweetheart,” Howard exclusively told E! News’ Lauren Herbert at the 2026 ELLE Women in Hollywood Celebration in Beverly Hills, Calif., Nov. 16. “He had worked prior to Twilight, but Twilight was really sort of his breakthrough role.”

“And the whole time, at least when I worked with him, he was so sincere and sweet and just the loveliest guy, like not into stardom or himself or anything,” she added. “Just an incredibly present person.”

While Pattinson’s Edward Cullen may have killed Howard’s Victoria in the 2010 film The Twilight Saga: Eclipse—which also starred Kristen Stewart and Taylor Lautner—there’s certainly no bad blood.

“He decapitated me,” the Jurassic World: Dominion star quipped. “Privilege and honor to be decapitated by Robert Pattinson.”

That’s because of the person Pattinson, 40, was when he wasn’t wearing the skin of a killer.

“He’s not schmoozy,” Howard explained. “He’s not trying to be cool. He's just who he is, and he happens to be absolutely gorgeous. But he's a true artist, and his career since Twilight has obviously demonstrated that a zillion times over.”

So, though Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, and Damson Idris were just a few stars who were rumored to be the next 007, it was The Odyssey actor who ultimately got the call to star in the new film helmed by his Dune: Part Three director Denis Villeneuve.

As Howard, 45, put it, “Him as James Bond feels really right.”

But the Primetime star is just one celeb getting their flowers from The Help star. After all, Howard presented Inde Navarrette with the Ralph Lauren Spotlight Award at the event.

"I don't even know who to liken her to because what she did is so utterly unique and singular,” Howard said, “I mean she's worked before Obsession, but Obsession is really her breakout role, and she arrived so fully formed.”

“It’s almost like Marilyn Monroe or something or Audrey Hepburn,” she continued. “She's an absolute icon already.”

Until Pattinson dominates the big screen as James Bond, keep reading to sink your teeth into Twilight’s best kept secrets…

1. When first writing Twilight, screenwriter Mark Lord recalled fears that the male audience wouldn't be interested. They wanted to take the concept of Romeo and Juliet, but with vampires "and build in a structure that was far more a cinematic structure," he shared on The Big Hit Show podcast in January 2022. "And they wanted to just put in more action to advance it more and give something more for the male audience. They thought they were going to lose the male audience with too much of a romance."

2. Director Catherine Hardwicke quickly made the writers pivot after throwing the first draft into the trash. "The original script literally had Bella on jet skis being chased by the FBI," she recalled. "She was a star athlete. Nothing to do with the book."

3. Paramount and MTV initially had acquired the film rights to Twilight, with the original script making significant changes to the book. "It had veered very far from the book, and so I did not like it at all," director Hardwicke revealed to CinemaBlend. After three years, Paramount released the rights and then-independent film studio Summit Entertainment immediately picked them up.

4. Book author Stephenie Meyer had some strict guidelines when it came to the adaptation of her source material. She didn't want any stereotypical vampire elements added in and demanded that Edward's "so the lion fell in love with the lamb" line make it into the final version.

She also stepped in to have Kellan Lutz take over the role of Emmett when she didn't agree with the initial casting choice and asked to have Bella and Edward's first kiss toned down. Of stepping in to put her foot down, Meyer told EW, "That's hard for me, but I'm glad of every time I did it and I don't think I stepped on too many toes and everyone seems to still like me."

5. According to Summit's then-Head of Production Erik Feig, Meyer was adamant that her vampires didn't have fangs. "The negotiated language says, 'No actor playing a vampire will have canine incisors longer than those found in the average human being,'" he recalled on Spotify's The Big Hit Show podcast. "And that to me is... I love that line."

6. Some soon-to-be-major actresses (including some who would become faces of their own respective franchises) that auditioned for Bella Swan included Emily Browning (Meyer's early first choice), Michelle Trachtenberg, Lily Collins and Jennifer Lawrence.

"I didn't really know what it was," Lawrence later said on The Howard Stern Show of her Twilight audition. "You just get like five pages [at the audition] and they're like, 'Act monkey.' And when it came out I was like, 'Hot damn. Whoa!'"

7. Based on a suggestion from Emile Hirsch, who starred opposite Kristen Stewart in Into the Wild and was in director Hardwicke's Lords of Dogtown, the filmmaker zeroed in on Stewart for the role.

"I see Kristen…with all that longing and just lusting for Emile [Hirsch] And I'm like, 'Oh my God, that is so what I felt from the book. This girl that has so much longing, and it's so contained, and just repressed longing, but it was so palpable,'" Hardwicke said of watching Stewart in Into the Wild. "So I thought, 'Oh, it's got to be Kristen.'"

8. The actress initially had no interest in the project upon hearing the synopsis, but after meeting with Hardwicke and going through the script together, Stewart quickly changed her mind.

9. Over 5,000 actors reportedly went out for the role of Edward Cullen, including Dave Franco, Jamie Campbell Bower (who would go on to play Caius in the follow-up films), Schitt's Creek's Dustin Milligan and Michael Welch (who landed the role of human Michael Newton). Moreover, Henry Cavill was Meyer's first choice, but was too old by the time the movie came along. He was reportedly considered for the role of Carlisle, the Cullen family patriarch.

But the final four contenders were Robert Pattinson, Ben Barnes, Shiloh Fernandez and Jackson Rathbone (who would eventually nab the role of Jasper Cullen), and they were all brought to Hardwicke's home in California to test opposite Stewart.

10. The chemistry read involved the infamous meadow scene, which Stewart and Pattinson performed on Hardwicke's bed. When it came to the kiss, Hardwicke recalled Pattinson being a bit too revved-up, but told EW, "It was electric." Pattinson later revealed he took half a Valium before the make-or-break audition.

After the four actors tested, Hardwicke was still uncertain, but Stewart knew who her Edward was right away, telling Vanity Fair, "I was like, "'Are you kidding me!? It's such an obvious choice!'"

11. Prior to landing Twilight, Pattinson had considered leaving the entertainment industry after a string of failed auditions following Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (RIP Cedric Diggory!). "I was going to quit [acting] because I never got any jobs," he would recall on Today, "so I guess it's not really quitting when you're not getting jobs—it's just surrendering to fate."

12. While he would go on to play the titular teen wolf in MTV's hit series Teen Wolf, Tyler Posey revealed he auditioned against his good friend Taylor Lautner for the role of Jacob Black in the first film. "So, yeah, I auditioned for Twilight, Jacob Black. Taylor Lautner beat me," he told MTV with a laugh. "Congratulations, dude. That's a sick role. That's awesome. I hate you."

13. Another young star who auditioned for a role in Twilight was future Pretty Little Liars actress Lucy Hale who wanted to play Alice Cullen (she would also audition for Jane in New Moon and Leah Clearwater in Eclipse). She told J-14, "I read the books and I wanted to be part of the first movie so bad."

14. After initially going out for the role of villain James, Cam Gigandet (known for his bad boy turn on The O.C.) was brought back in to read for Emmett Cullen. "So I was like, 'Is there anything you guys have for me? Anything at all?' And so I went in for Kellan Lutz's character," he told MTV. "Once I went in, I was like, 'Oh my gosh, I like this character, but I just have to play James.' We waited a little bit, and after about a week, we heard back, and they were like, 'OK, we'll give him the job.'"

15. Meyer made a brief cameo in the first film as one of the diners in a scene between Bella and her dad Charlie (Billy Burke). She would also appear in Breaking Dawn: Part 1 as a guest as Bella and Edward's wedding, along with screenwriter Melissa Rosenberg, co-producer Bill Bannerman and producer Wyck Godfrey.

16. "On the first shot on the first day I strained one of my ass cheeks, my ass just couldn't take the strain of the first one," Pattinson revealed to Jimmy Kimmel . His injury caused a problem with the company insuring the film and led to a bit of physical therapy for the star.

17. When New Moon was officially announced the day after Twilight dominated its opening night at the box office, fans were shocked to see Lautner not listed among the cast members. But it wasn't a typo, as the studio confirmed it was assessing whether or not the 16-year-old could play the character after his wolf transformation.

"The doubts came up because he had very few scenes in the first movie, and also because he's described as being 6-foot-5 in the second book, so there were reasonable facts that we had to come to grips with," New Moon director Chris Weitz explained to Reuters of the 5-foot-9 star.

18. In fact, there was even an actor in mind to take over the part: The Scorpion King 2 and One Tree Hill star Michael Copon. "I have nothing against Taylor personally. I think he's great and tremendous at what he does," Copon told MTV. "But it's just adjusting to the fact that Jacob has to grow. It's a matter of going with the storyline."

19. But Lautner was committed to playing Jacob, taking on an intense training regime to bulk up as soon as production wrapped on the first film. His prep included consuming 4,000 calories per day, eating every two hours and working out for two hours at least five days a week.

"I knew I had to get to work right away; there could be no waiting involved," the then-17-year-old told Interview. "The day I finished Twilight, I came home and started bulking up. For New Moon, I'm 30 pounds heavier than I was in Twilight."

20. While Lautner (and his legions of fans) enjoyed his physical transformation, there was one aspect to playing Jacob that the actor didn't like: that wig. "There was hatred between both of us," he told MTV. "It did not like me, I did not like it. Not fond memories."

21. After dyeing her hair blonde to play Cullen family member Rosalie in the first film, Nikki Reed opted to wear a wig for the rest of the series to protect her hair. "My hair fell out," she revealed to MTV of the damage. "It took 36 hours initially to make me blond, and every other day, I was bleaching my head and my skin. This time around, we are testing out different wigs and stuff."

22. More wig woes: After cutting her hair to play Joan Jett in The Runaways, Stewart had to wear a wig for Eclipse, one that earned a lot of eyebrow-raises. Leading up to Breaking Dawn: Part 1, Stewart assured fans she would be rocking her own hair and revealed Summit really didn't want her to chop her hair in the first place.

"They're going to hate me for this, but they offered me lots of ridiculous... many ridiculous things to not do that," she told George Lopez in 2010. "I completely understand, I just thought we'd have a better...wig, and, uh, it's OK, we worked it out, and hopefully, hopefully, hopefully, it's OK now."

23. After originating the role of villain vamp Victoria, Rachelle Levefre was replaced by Bryce Dallas Howard (who was first approached to take on the role years prior) in Eclipse. And Levefre was not happy about the casting change, which the studio attributed to scheduling conflicts.

"I was stunned by Summit's decision to recast the role," Levefre said in a statement. "I was fully committed to the Twilight saga, and to the portrayal of Victoria."

24. Newcomer Xavier Samuel won the role of Riley, Victoria's sidekick, in the franchise's third installment, reportedly beating out Channing Tatum and Harry Potter star Tom Felton for the job.

25. Michael Sheen took on the role of Volturi coven leader Aro because his daughter Lily (with Kate Beckinsale) was a massive fan of the series. "I was mainly excited about it because I knew I would make my daughter very happy," he told The Daily Record. "That was the main reason, and then I read the books and I really enjoyed them. I didn't think I was going to, but I really did."

26. For Bella's highly anticipated wedding dress, production turned to Carolina Herrera. "Carolina had worked with Stephenie personally for events. And they'd struck up a friendship and dialogue so we talked to Carolina for the dress," costume designer Michael Wilkinson revealed to MTV. "They'd been talking about the day that this dress would hit the big screen for a while and I was happy to help with the design as a consultant because it had to work with the rest of the film."

For the rest of the Cullen women and Bella's mom, the costume designer created original dresses for each character.

27. The problem with a custom couture wedding gown? The chances were high of it getting ruined—which almost happened due to the bad weather in Oregon—and they only had two duplicates.

"I had a vision of the wet paint slowly creeping up the hem of the dress, but in the end, we got away with it," Wilkinson told InStyle. "We shot the wide shot first, and sure enough, by the time we moved in for the close-ups, the hem was soaking up the paint like a thirsty sponge!"

28. Okay, but how did Edward get Bella pregnant when he's, you know, dead, and she's not? Meyer actually provided an answer to this question on her official website back in the day: "Like with vampire skin—which looks similar to human skin and has the same basic function—fluids closely related to seminal fluids still exist in male vampires, which carry genetic information and are capable of bonding with a human ovum." So there you go.

29. The original cut of Bella and Edward's wedding night sex scene initially caused Breaking Dawn: Part 1 to receive an R-rating, with director Bill Condor forced to tone down the couple's highly awaited first time. "There are very specific guidelines on thrusting intercourse," he told The Hollywood Reporter.

30. Pattinson nearly caused the fanbase to combust in 2011 when he revealed at a press conference for Breaking Dawn that a real priest was used for the wedding scene, "So technically we are already married because he did all the things you would do in a normal ceremony," he explained. "So we don't have a civil union in law, but I guess in the church we are actually married."

31. After Stewart wore a B.B. Dakota coat in the first film, the clothing company rebranded it as "the Bella Swan jacket." Summit swiftly filed a legal claim and in 2011, a judge ruled in their favor.

32. Stars you may have forgotten appeared in the franchise's films include Anna Kendrick, Shameless' Noel Fisher, Lost star Maggie Grace, Lee Pace, Westworld's Angela Sarafyan and Oscar winner Rami Malek. In fact, Kendrick kind of forgot she was in the series. "Holy s--t," she tweeted in 2018. "I just remembered I was in Twilight."

33. In an interview with Vulture years later, Hardwicke didn't exactly have fond memories of her time reading the scripts for Twilight, admitting, "Every one of those scripts sucked. Oh Lord, did they suck." She isn't the only franchise director to bash the series, with David Slade having to apologize for disparaging comments he made before signing on to direct Eclipse. "Twilight drunk? No, not even drunk. Twilight on acid? No, not even on acid? Twilight at gun point? Just shoot me," he once said during a radio interview.

34. A 10 year-old Mackenzie Foy landed the integral role of Renesmee, Bella and Edward's half-vampire half-human baby that Jacob imprints on (LOL remember that?). And the entire production team and cast were protective of the newcomer on the set of Breaking Dawn: Part 2. To protect the tween, director Condor placed a swear jar on set (it accumulated more than $800!) and the two leads went just a bit meta.

"They were amazing with her," Condor told EW. "It really brought something paternal out in Rob, and Kristen was especially protective. I'd have to interrupt them when they were in deep conversation to get going with a scene."

While CGI was ultimately used to portray the baby version of Renesmee, it was later revealed the production team attempted to use a doll to extremely creepy results. Seriously, it earned the nickname Chuckesmee.

#883. Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

#882. Blackburn boss Mowbray steps back over health issues

Tony Mowbray's last game in charge of Blackburn Rovers was an impressive 2-1 win over West Ham United before November's international break

Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.

The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.

Mowbray had previously taken time out of the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

Rovers said Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds would take responsibility for first-team duties "for the time being".

BBC Sport was initially told Mowbray had "stepped down" but we have since been updated that he has "stepped back". No further details have been given although the club are not thought to be looking for a successor.

"Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers," Mowbray said in a statement., external

"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.

"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.

"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."

Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.

They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.

The announcement comes before Sunday's Lancashire derby against Burnley at Turf Moor, which was set to be Mowbray's 900th game in management as well as his 63rd birthday.

Mowbray has been in management for over two decades and his first spell at Blackburn ended at the conclusion of the 2021-22 season when he was eventually replaced by Jon Dahl Tomasson.

He subsequently held roles with Sunderland, Birmingham and a second spell with West Bromwich Albion before his return to Ewood Park.

In his first spell at Blackburn, he could not halt the club's relegation from the Championship, yet he led them to promotion back from League One at the first attempt and subsequently re-established them in the second tier.

In February 2024, he had been diagnosed with cancer but was eventually given the all-clear following treatment.

He leaves with Blackburn in better shape than they were during a tumultuous 2025-26 campaign, which finished with Michael O'Neill opting not to take the manager's job on a full-time basis and instead choosing to remain as boss of Northern Ireland.

"Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much," Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood added.

"Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can."

Tony Mowbray won seven of his 17 matches (D3 L7) in charge of Blackburn in all competitions in the 2026-27 campaign

Mowbray's decision was communicated to the club's playing and coaching staff at the Brockhall training ground on Tuesday morning by chief executive Curwood and chief operating officer Suhail Shaikh.

Staff based at Ewood Park, as well as those working remotely and at other club sites, were also informed before the news was made public.

The announcement was met with understandable concern from players, who are supportive of Mowbray's decision.

A number have since paid tribute to the 62-year-old on social media, thanking him for his support and guidance, with some having worked under him during two separate spells at the club.

Rovers remain in close contact with Mowbray and his family and continue to offer their full support.

#881. Where Hunger Games’ Jena Malone Believes Johanna Mason Is Now

Ahead of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premiere, Jena Malone, who played Johanna Mason in the original series, shared where her character is now in an exclusive E! News interview.

Jena Malone thinks her Hunger Games character is still making them pay for it.

Over 10 years after The Hunger Games: Mockingjay—Part 2 hit theaters, Malone, who played District 7 victor Johanna Mason, revealed her hopes for where she ended up after the Panem revolution.

“I would love her to be like deep in the forest,” Malone told E! News in an exclusive interview at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premiere in New York Nov. 16. “Training women to do somatic warrior, like healing exercises to sort of exercise their grief.”

Given her character’s fierce personality, the Saved alum admitted that Johanna would likely “have her own army basically.”

But as she’s looking ahead at Johanna’s journey, the film franchise itself is winding the clock back with the new film, set 25 years before fans met Malone’s character.

For the actress, it was “really lovely” to reunite with former costars like Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Woody Harrelson, Elizabeth Banks and Willow Shields at the Sunrise on the Reaping premiere.

“It’s kind of like a homecoming,” she mused. “I feel like you get to see long lost friends. The fanbase, I feel like their enthusiasm never changes.”

And considering the upcoming film will follow a young Haymitch Abernathy—with Joseph Zada taking over the role from Harrelson—during the 50th Hunger Games, Malone considered that an origin story for her character may feature another fan favorite: District 4 victor Finnick Odair, who was played by Sam Claflin.

“It would have to be Johanna and Finnick,” she posited. “‘Cause they were in a similar game.”

Nevertheless, Malone is admittedly more interested in the reconstruction of Panem after the revolution.

“What happened to the Capitol after?” Malone considered. “I’m interested. I love when governments get overthrown, but I’m also wildly fascinated with what comes next. How do we rebuild?”

Zada, for his part, might know what lies ahead for his character Haymitch after the upcoming prequel—which hits theaters Nov. 20—but he shared he is at a loss for words after going through his own experience alongside McKenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons and more.

“I don’t know how to feel,” he told E! News in a separate interview. “It feels so full circle.”

He emphasized, “I’m just so proud—I could cry right now.”

As a lifelong Hunger Games fan, Grace similarly joked that she’s been asking herself, ‘Real or Not Real?’ since scoring her dream job as Maysilee Donner.

“It’s very strange to be here and to be part of this in any regard,” she told E! on the red carpet. “It does not feel real. This is constantly like a dream I’ll wake up from. I feel so thankful.”

#880. Danny Kelly obituary

Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work

Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football.

In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur.

Kelly’s deputy at the NME, Stuart Maconie, described how he championed “the best of everything … roots, rock, reggae, the Smiths, Tamla Motown, the Clash, T.Rex, prog”. His close friend Danny Baker, his regular co-host since 1992, said that they shared “music, football, life … an absurd private universe of turmoil” together and turned to humour “to forge another path for football punditry, based in hoopla, voodoo and toasters”.

Kelly’s much-shared 2008 commentary of an Arsenal and Spurs match, alongside the retired footballer Stan Collymore, exemplified his relatable passion: “I love football, Stan! I love it!” he shouted when Spurs equalised, adding, seconds later, “How unprofessional.” Collymore described how Kelly brought him to TalkSport after he struggled with chronic mental health issues; Kelly gave many others support during their own physical and psychological struggles.

Born in London, into a family that had recently emigrated from County Carlow in Ireland to Islington, Danny was the oldest of the six children of Josie (nee Martin), a school dinner lady, and Andy, a railway worker.

Despite growing up “literally in the shadow of Highbury Stadium”, and in a family of Arsenal supporters, Danny supported their near-rivals. Speaking to FourFourTwo magazine in 2006, he said that Spurs represented “the true spirit of rock’n’roll”.

A pupil at Sacred Heart primary school in Holloway and later at St Aloysius’ College in Highgate, Kelly loved history (“but I don’t suppose anyone really cares about my opinions about the Anglo-Prussian agreements of the 17th century,” he told the New York Times’ sports website The Athletic in 2022).

In a 2020 interview with the Behind the Lines podcast, he described himself as “teenage music fanatic”, calling the NME in the mid-1970s his “bible”.

After failing to complete law and combined arts studies at Leicester University through “lack of effort, and punk rock”, he worked at British Rail on the complaints counter and as a station announcer. As a shop steward with the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, he wrote about music in the union magazine. A copy picked up by the NME jazz critic Richard Cook at a TUC conference in 1983 led to freelance work for Kelly, who then returned to college to pursue media studies at the Polytechnic of Central London (now the University of Westminster).

His writing was ebullient and vivid: Marvin Gaye possessed “a combination of gifts seldom stuffed into one body, one psyche”; the Smiths made “a Catherine wheel of inspired language” against “shifting, sometimes unnervingly evocative and beautiful guitar music”. Joining the NME in 1985 as a writer, he became deputy editor in 1987 and editor in 1990, before taking over Q in 1992.

There, he commanded audiences in the office and at after-work pub sessions regaling his stories of meeting musicians, and presented serious cover stars with characteristic irreverence: Sting, formerly of the Police, in handcuffs; Kate Bush under the headline “Booze, fags, blokes and me”.

In 1995, he launched Total Sport magazine, which ran for four years, and from 1997 to 1998 presented the late-night Channel 4 sports and entertainment show Under the Moon. Simultaneously, he ran editorial operations for Football 365, which became popular during the 1998 World Cup.

His subsequent radio career was prolific and popular. On TalkSport’s This Sporting Life, his interviewees included Virginia Wade, Frank Bruno and Eric Bristow. Trans Euro Express combined his love of European football and music, while his expertise in other sports, including cycling and American football, was in regular demand.

A year-long marriage ended in 1998; in 2005, the literary journalist and editor Alex Clark became his partner. He married her, wearing shoes from a range by his favourite rapper, MF Doom, in 2021. They moved to Kilkenny in 2018 to be near his mother, who had returned to Ireland.

Kelly broadcast remotely throughout the pandemic, up until his diagnosis with oesophageal cancer in March. He posted a diary of his treatment, the Kelly Cancer Kronikles, to his 106,000 followers on X until August, its title referencing one of his literary heroes, the fictional schoolboy Nigel Molesworth.

“I hope that what I’ve done over the years is to be honest and open about football, life, culture, everything else,” he said to the Athletic, and added the only two pieces of advice he ever gave to aspiring broadcasters. “Be a version of yourself, but add an extra 15% of personality. And don’t be shit. Try not to be shit and you’ll be OK.”

Alex, his mother, Josie, and his siblings, Margaret, Michael, Andrew, Joanna and John, survive him.

Daniel John Kelly, journalist and broadcaster, born 22 December 1956; died 10 November 2026

#879. Romario demands Ancelotti sacking as war of words continues

Few would have predicted that Carlo Ancelotti would be facing the wrath of a Brazil legend just 18 months into his tenure as head coach of the national team.

But Romario, Brazil's fourth-highest scorer behind only Neymar, Pele and Ronaldo, has publicly demanded legendary manager Ancelotti be relieved of his duties twice in the past week.

It all started after Brazil suffered a 3-2 friendly defeat by Japan on Friday thanks to a controversial stoppage-time winner from Tatsuhiro Sakamoto.

Ancelotti received a red card for dissent in the aftermath - the first of his international management career, as Barcelona forward Raphinha also saw red.

And after Brazil's friendly defeat, Romario took to social media to air his frustrations about the former Real Madrid boss.

"Ancelotti, enough is enough! Pack your bags and leave!" he wrote on Instagram.

"Nobody questions your history. You are one of the greatest coaches world football has ever seen, but that was at club level."

Brazil were eliminated by Norway in the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup, meaning they failed to qualify for the quarter-finals for the first time since 1990.

And Romario alluded to this too, stating the country "can't take the risk of throwing another World Cup in the trash - the time to act is now!"

The Brazil boss has been in the game long enough to know how to deal with all sorts of opinions.

Ancelotti has won the Champions League a record five times as a head coach and won the league title in all of Europe's top five divisions, along with multiple domestic cups.

But his record with Brazil is far from perfect. Across 21 matches, they have recorded 12 wins, four draws and five defeats.

However, while Ancelotti acknowledges the need for improvement, he emphasised the fact that it is still "a new project".

Speaking before Brazil's friendly with Singapore on Tuesday the Italian said: "In a democratic country with freedom of speech, everyone is allowed to express their opinion.

"It's not up to me to say whether the things he says are correct, wrong or just stupid. The truth is that Romario talks a lot. A lot. It's his right."

Despite the criticism he has faced, Ancelotti feels Brazil are on the right track - and who is to tell him otherwise when you look at his track record?

"I really like what we're doing," he said.

You would have thought that would have been enough to let it lie for the time being.

But before Brazil had even kicked a ball in their next friendly against Singapore, Romario was speaking out again.

The former striker, who is the ninth-highest scorer in football history with 784 goals, doubled down on his calls for Ancelotti to be sacked.

"I talk a lot because when it comes to the national team, I have size, weight and power of speech," Romario, 60, said.

"I do not speak to gain followers, I do not speak for people to like me. I speak my mind.

"I have worn this shirt for many years and I am pretty sure I was one of the ones that helped the 'little yellow' be respected all over the world."

He said he respected Ancelotti but added he hadn't "added anything new" to the national side.

"I will say it again: resign! We will find another coach who will do a better job than you.

"And I'm saying this to your face, not through a message, including to the president of the [Brazilian Football Confederation], who is long overdue to fire you."

Brazil faced Singapore in their final match of 2026 on Tuesday and won 7-0.

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior, who has come under scrutiny of his own so far this season, scored a hat-trick within the opening 21 minutes while Bournemouth winger Rayan and Chelsea's Estevao were also on the scoresheet.

That result that may bring a pause to proceedings in this war of words for now.

However, if this past seven days has proved anything, it is that this saga is likely far from over.

"It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star.

The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153.

GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement. "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself."

The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position."

After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun.

MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney said.

The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #876. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

#875. Millwall open disciplinary proceedings against Baker

Baker featured in five Premier League games for Brighton in the 2023-24 season

Millwall are undertaking disciplinary proceedings against forward Benicio Baker following social media posts critical of senior figures at the club, BBC Sport understands.

The 22-year-old winger has played only for the Lions' under-21 side since joining from Brighton in February 2025 on a long-term deal.

BBC Sport understands the proceedings relate to a number of off-field matters, including social media activity.

Posts attributed to Baker's account, which has since been deactivated on Instagram but has been widely republished, appeared critical of senior figures at Millwall and suggested he "can't even train with the (under) 21s".

It is understood Baker was initially unavailable because of injury, but he is now the subject of disciplinary proceedings which, in the most serious circumstances, could lead to the cancellation of his contract.

Baker is also understood to be exploring options away from Millwall.

At the height of his career, Baker made six first-team appearances for Brighton under former manager Roberto de Zerbi, including in the Premier League.

The England Under-20 international also spent time in the academy systems at West Ham and Porto before making 14 senior appearances on loan as Port Vale finished second in League Two in 2024.

While at West Ham, before joining Porto, he was linked with moves to overseas clubs including Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Benfica.

Millwall have declined to comment, while representatives for Baker have been contacted.

#874. Julia Garner Reunites With Anna Delvey After Inventing Anna Role

Four years after Julia Garner played disgraced criminal socialite Anna Delvey in Netflix’s Inventing Anna, the actress and her muse reunited at a screening for The Altruists in New York.

VIP is always better, but this reunion is simply the best.

Four years after Julia Garner’s Emmy-winning portrayal of Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna, the actress reunited with the fake socialite at a fan screening for The Altruists.

At the Nov. 16 event for the Netflix series—which chronicles the rise and fall of the now-incarcerated FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and exec Caroline Ellison—Garner and Delvey shared a warm moment together on the red carpetat the Paris Theater in New York. In fact, the convicted con artist (real name Anna Sorokin) even joined in on the question and answer segment with the Ozark alum and Altruists creator Graham Moore on stage.

Delvey, for her part, was looking as chic as ever, sporting a black skirt suit with a fitted blazer, tights and her blonde hair styled into a swoopy lob. Of course, the 35-year-old also sported a required accessory with her ankle monitor wrapped around her left leg. (Delvey is currently under a flexible house arrest from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement following her 2021 release from prison.)

Garner, for her part, matched Delvey’s color palette in a halter knee-length dress with an attached long-sleeved cover.

And while it’s been years since Garner portrayed Delvey on screen in the Netflix series, the duo’s history dates back even further to when Garner visited Delvey during her nearly four-year prison sentence following her conviction of grand larceny.

“She was very nice,” Delvey said of Garner’s visit during a 2022 appearance on the Forbidden Fruits podcast. “She came to see me and she’s a very sweet girl.”

Nevertheless, Delvey had one problem with Garner’s take on her: her iconic accent.

“It's just so weird,” she admitted, “because the way you hear yourself—like your voice is just completely different when you hear yourself on TV.”

Still, Delvey defended Garner’s artistic liberties.

“She was portraying me from like, 2015, 2016, 2017,” the Dancing with the Stars alum explained. “So now I've spent the past four years just in the States. I was surrounded by Americans so maybe my accent was different.”

To Delvey, her voice has evolved even since her prison sentence.

“I barely even speak German these days,” she said. “All I speak is English. Back in the day, I would speak French, German, English on a daily basis.”

It looks like 'The Martian,' but due to international copyright laws, it's not.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like "The Martian," doesn't it?

There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base.

That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls.

Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving "Event Horizon", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me.

There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027".

You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist.

Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging.

There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike.

The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men.

Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars?

I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish "Routine." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.

Ian is the Entertainment Editor at Space.com, covering movies, TV series, and games in the space and sci-fi realms. He's a massive sci-fi nerd and has been writing about games and entertainment for over eight years, with articles on sites like Space, LiveScience, GamesRadar, and more. With a degree in biology, a PhD in chemistry, and his previous role at the Institute of Physics Publishing, Ian is taking a world tour through the different scientific disciplines.

#872. Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’

In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations

I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

We felt unwelcome from the moment we arrived and we were not the only team to experience this. Nigeria exploited all avenues to play mind games with their opposition and to make them lose focus on the matches.

We arrived early in the morning at the Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos and faced our first test: how to retrieve our luggage. Only one carousel was working, which meant we had to wait a long time for our bags to arrive. We had a training session planned for later in the day and were all eager to get to the hotel, settle in and prepare for our first practice.

As we stepped out the airport doors, we looked for the bus that was to take us there, but we didn’t see one anywhere. As players, we were irritable and impatient, and starting to show it. Some of us were slumped on our bags, others had taken up residence on the pavement, and we were all cranky, especially as it took over an hour before a bus arrived.

Like in Mozambique a few years before, the bus was too small. Another 21-seater and we were 27 – 20 players and seven support staff, as well as all our luggage. Luckily, most of us had experience of how to squeeze in and so we knew the drill. We also had the advantage of our bags travelling in a smaller vehicle behind the bus, so the only challenge was fitting all the bodies in.

Generally, we saw the lighter side of these things and laughed as some of us got comfortable on the floor and others had to make do with a teammate’s lap. But we lost our sense of humour when we realised we had no air-conditioning and the drive was going to last at least another hour. Some grumbling ensued, but we knew better than to complain at such an early stage, and it seemed that things would get better soon.

When we got to the hotel, the building that greeted us looked fairly new from the outside, with freshly painted walls and a manicured garden at the entrance. But when we walked through the doors, it looked as though the hotel was in the process of being renovated, and the outside was clearly the bit that had been made up first. It still looked like a decent place, so we weren’t too worried, and the smell of new paint and the sight of workers installing lights made us feel special as the first group of people staying in this hotel.

All of us were looking forward to being in our rooms and the chance to shower and relax before training. It was only when I saw maintenance workers carrying still-sealed mattresses to the rooms that it occurred to me that we were being put up in a hotel that was not fully ready for guests. I was only half-right. Actually, it was not ready at all.

When we got to our rooms, they were empty: no mattresses on the beds, no lightbulbs in the lamps and, worst of all, not a drop of water in the taps. This made us all a little worried, but we were told it would be sorted out as soon as we had finished our training. We did have lunch at the hotel, although by now I was suspicious of things and particularly of the spread of fish and chicken, and then left for training. At least that went smoothly, and we expected to get back to suitable accommodation. No such luck.

We returned to beds being made but still had no lights or running water. After a training session in extremely warm conditions, we were all dripping with sweat from head to toe and we had to make another plan. A few of our players spotted a river just outside the hotel and said they were going to go there to rinse themselves off. I thought they were joking.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

When I looked again, the players had stripped down to their tights and sports bras, wrapped themselves in their pristine white hotel towels with their toiletries in hand and were heading out the door. If I wanted to be clean, I realised, I had to join them. My hesitation was twofold: I had never washed in a river before and wasn’t sure whether it was hygienic, but I was also still quite young and didn’t want to expose my body in public. I had to get over my qualms quite quickly. Fortunately, we didn’t have to wash in the river again. No one knows how, but when we opened the taps the following day, the water gushed out.

With that kind of preparation, and Nigeria being as strong a team as they were, it was hardly a surprise that we lost 2-0. We experienced Nigeria’s off the field tactics first-hand. I did have one happy memory from the match, though. The Nigerian centre-back, Onome Ebi, who would go on to become the first African to play in six World Cups between 2003 and 2023, gave me her jersey. We both wore No 5 and she was the first international to give me her shirt. Given how much my Banyana Banyana jersey meant to me, I understood how special and symbolic this moment was, and I have stored it in my memory to this day.

This is an edited extract from 185: The Janine van Wyk Story is published by Karavan Press and available on Amazon in the United Kingdom.

#871. Why always him? The rise and fall of Balotelli

Why always him? The rise and fall of Balotelli

Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.

Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.

The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah.

Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history.

Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.

Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.

A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.

It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.

The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.

Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.

Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.

There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".

The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.

Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.

Balotelli played for Mancini at Inter and Manchester City - and was briefly recalled for Italy by his old boss in 2018

Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City.

Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.

A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.

Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.

After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.

Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."

Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.

In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.

BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.

Mario Balotelli scored 30 goals in 80 games for Manchester City

Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United, celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.

There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person Â£1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.

True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.

A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".

On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City's title bid.

But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.

Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.

"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."

But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?

Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.

The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.

Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.

"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."

Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.

"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.

"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.

"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

'Why always me?' - relive that Balotelli moment in huge Man City win

'Balotelli to Barnsley? Now that is one Mario story I don't believe'

Balotelli never threatened to have an international career to rival Ronaldo or Messi.

But there were still moments that linger in the memory.

He became the first black player to feature for Italy at a major tournament when he starred at Euro 2012.

And, more than that, he hit three goals to finish as the tournament's joint top scorer - with five others - as Italy lost to Spain in the final.

An abiding image is that of a shirtless Balotelli flexing his muscles after scoring the goal that sent the Azzurri to the final, with a 2-1 win against Germany.

Balotelli's celebration against Germany in the Euro 2012 semi-finals became an iconic image of the tournament

Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.

Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.

While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.

Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.

In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.

Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.

Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.

Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.

The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.

Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."

Mancini told AC Milan that Balotelli could become one of the world's best while in Serie A.

A glut of goals followed the striker's return to the San Siro in January 2013, before a surprising move back to the Premier League followed 18 months later.

Liverpool had been impressed, but Balotelli's spell on Merseyside would prove forgettable for all. One goal in 16 Premier League games under Brendan Rodgers was not what was expected from the Â£16m buy.

The failed transfer sparked a loan move back to Milan, where injuries hampered his progress. When it was time for Balotelli to return to Merseyside, Jurgen Klopp had arrived and said the striker would not be part of his Liverpool plans.

Balotelli later called the move to Anfield "the worst mistake of my life".

Steven Gerrard and Mario Balotelli were briefly Liverpool team-mates - but it didn't work out at Anfield for the Italian

Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?

Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.

Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.

And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.

It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.

But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.

"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.

"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.

"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.

"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.

"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."

#870. Switzerland roll over sorry Scotland to increase the pressure on Pocognoli

A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment had arrived in different circumstances.

A second-string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous. “I don’t think you’ve got time in international football,” said Robertson as dust settled here. Ouch.

This was a horrible night for Pocognoli, who is under serious pressure just three months into his tenure. Scotland’s players looked a disillusioned and disorganised lot. Pocognoli has never previously managed in international football, which renders it reasonable to ask his qualifications to improve this grim scenario. Scotland have finished a distant third in a favourable Nations League section. Ramifications exist for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in December. Pocognoli is taking a pounding in the court of public opinion.

“The score is painful,” said Pocognoli. “I see a lot of good things in the way that we try to play. The result is heavy but the players gave everything. They enjoy playing like this.” An eye test suggests otherwise. Scotland are overly generous in defence, lame in midfield and powder-puff in attack. It is quite the mix.

Pocognoli’s demeanour during pre-match media duties suggested he was irritated by the early questioning of his approach. The Belgian is unwilling to deviate from the deployment of three centre-backs whether Scotland are at home to North Macedonia or away to Switzerland. While the prospect of facing a highly impressive Swiss team would ordinarily make Scots gulp, there was cause for hope in St Gallen. Not only had Switzerland already won Group B1 but they were in makeshift form.

Switzerland’s lack of cohesion was apparent during an opening spell where the visitors looked decent. A flurry of set pieces and a John McGinn half volley that dipped over Yvon Mvogo’s crossbar emphasised Scottish attacking intent. On a difficult pitch, Switzerland’s first 20 minutes lacked purpose. As good as things were to get for Scotland, alas.

There appeared no real danger as Zachary Athekame fired in a hopeful cross from the Swiss right. Scotland had an abundance of cover inside their own penalty area. The problem was that one of those charged with clearing lines, Lewis Ferguson, instead poked the ball past Angus Gunn. No own goals are pretty; this one was especially ugly. Ferguson had needlessly panicked.

Scotland attempted an immediate response as Aaron Hickey headed wide. The Brentford man had to be withdrawn before the interval, apparently damaging his left hamstring when making a defensive intervention.

Hickey, whose career has been seriously disrupted by injury, was understandably distraught. Although Switzerland were by now in control, McGinn spurned a glorious opportunity five minutes before the interval when heading straight at Mvogo. Adrian Bajrami spared McGinn’s blushes with an even worse miss at the opposite end before the teams headed for their orange wedges. The half had been humdrum in nature.

Ferguson shanking the ball out for a Switzerland corner set the tone for a spell where the game was put firmly out of Scotland’s reach. Samuel Ballet burst forward from midfield before playing a one-two with Remo Freuler and slamming towards the Scotland net. The ball was heading in before Winsley Boteli made certain, with the video assistant referee dismissing Scotland’s appeals for offside. The ease with which Ballet evaded those in navy blue was as striking as the space Freuler found himself in. Scotland’s structure, once a staple, was nonexistent. Five defenders and two deep lying midfielders were being gleefully ignored by the rampaging Swiss.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Number three was another Scotland horror show. Nathan Patterson was dispossessed by Boteli. The forward found Alvyn Sanches, who angled a shot across Gunn. So, so easy. Gunn’s positioning was questionable.

Scott McTominay, again peripheral, slammed over when it looked easier to notch a Scotland consolation. Scottish fans jeered after one sideways pass too many in defence. Many headed for the exit as Zeki Amdouni’s shot deflected off Luke Graham and beyond Gunn.

A year ago, Scotland were celebrating World Cup qualification on the most epic of Hampden Park nights as Denmark were vanquished. It is so difficult to square that occasion with 90 minutes in St Gallen. Scotland look a team in ghastly regression.
